findings.claim: MCDP 1's dissent-before, support-after rule and its refusal of yes-men are the most direct material in the corpus on the timing of disagreement.
findings.failure_mode: Superlative claim about the whole corpus that no deep reference supports; the corpus holds a named practice on the same move.
findings.evidence: mcdp1-warfighting-deep.md line 113 supports the dissent-then-support rule itself. The ranking against the rest of the corpus has no support: open-practice-library-deep.md line 219 carries the practice 'Disagree and Commit' (moving a team from disagreement to committed execution, with agreed review points and short delivery periods 'so that disagreement is short-lived'), and line 272 pairs it with 'Dissent Cards'. The distillation's Integration table also omits the Open Practice Library.
findings.fix: correct: MCDP 1's dissent-before, support-after rule and its refusal of yes-men say when disagreement is due and when it ends; the Open Practice Library's Disagree and Commit is the team-practice counterpart.

findings.section: Key Concepts for Stakeholder-Engagement (9, Main effort)
findings.claim: the harmonising question for every subordinate facing a decision is "How can I best support the main effort?"
findings.failure_mode: Detail taken from the converted source that the deep reference does not carry.
findings.evidence: Deep line 151 carries only 'The harmonising question every subordinate must ask: "How can I best support the main effort?"'. The qualifier 'facing a decision' comes from the converted source, lines 3800-3802: 'Like the commander's intent, the main effort becomes a harmonizing force for subordinate initiative. Faced with a decision, we ask ourselves: How can I best support the main effort?' The claim is true to the source, but it bypasses the deep ref.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: "Like the commander's intent, the main effort becomes a harmonizing force for subordinate initiative. Faced with a decision, we ask ourselves: How can I best support the main effort?" [V] (Ch 4, "Main effort"; converted source lines 3800-3802)

findings.section: Questions to Ask During Stakeholder-Engagement, Phase 7: Post-engagement
findings.claim: | Model admitting mistakes | Did the most senior person admit a mistake first, so that others could admit theirs? | Ch 3, "Training" |
findings.failure_mode: The source-tag points to a passage whose lever is different: the need label and question make senior-first admission look like the doctrine's mechanism.
findings.evidence: Deep line 115 (Ch 3, 'Training'): 'a subordinate's willingness to admit mistakes depends on the commander's willingness to tolerate them.' The doctrine's lever is the commander's tolerance of admitted mistakes, not the commander admitting first. The same technique in What to Look For (line 135) and the Worked Example (line 175) is plainly the distillation's own and is not attributed, so only this table row drifts.
findings.fix: correct: | Show that mistakes are tolerated | Did the most senior person make it plain that admitted mistakes would be tolerated (for example, by admitting one of their own first), so that others could admit theirs? | Ch 3, "Training" |
